source.title: Forecast collapse of transformer-based models under squared loss in financial time series

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives its own theoretical comparison of a simple linear predictor with a richer class containing interpolating predictors, and reports a PatchTST-versus-linear evaluation. The theoretical result challenges the claim that risk improves again for a more expressive interpolating class; however, it does not trace a double-descent curve.
record.gate_note: The paper does not sweep model size across an interpolation threshold, training epochs, or sample size, and does not locate a peak. It reports a theoretical interpolator-versus-linear comparison, an empirical PatchTST-versus-linear comparison, and a qualitative statement that increasing capacity widened the performance gap. Citations to other studies are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The paper mentions double descent only to set its own regime apart. Its theory compares a single 1-NN-type interpolator with a one-parameter linear predictor. It never varies capacity through or past an interpolation threshold, so it cannot show whether risk improves again beyond that point. Showing that one interpolator beats a simple model, or loses to it, does not bear on V4's claim about the shape of the curve. The PatchTST results compare two predictors and give no sizes, training error or interpolation status. The statement that larger capacity widened the gap is qualitative.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that more capacity and more data push ERM toward the trivial Bayes predictor (flat prices, zero returns). Excess error from expressive models is variance caused by noise reuse, and its magnitude grows with capacity. They argue progress requires changing the learning objective or the prediction target, not the architecture.
record.recipe_differences: The paper's theoretical comparison is between a simple linear predictor and a nearest-neighbor-type interpolator, with a separate PatchTST experiment. It does not reproduce the original double-descent size, epoch, or sample-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper qualitatively says the performance gap widened with increased model capacity, but gives no sizes or numerical results for those preliminary experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Under a martingale target, a 1-NN-type interpolating predictor has expected trajectory error of at least 2Hσ². A one-parameter linear ERM predictor has Hσ² + O(Hσ²/n).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: When the Bayes predictor is trivial and noise dominates, an interpolating nearest-neighbour predictor has roughly double the irreducible error of a simple well-specified predictor.

fits_no_version.finding: On EUR/USD 30-second data, PatchTST's test risk ratio to a linear benchmark is about 1.71. It has larger error on about 92% of windows (the text also says 94%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In weakly predictable financial trajectory forecasting, PatchTST underperforms a simple linear benchmark on most test windows.

fits_no_version.finding: The paper says that in preliminary experiments, larger PatchTST capacity widened the gap to the linear benchmark. No numbers are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In EUR/USD forecasting, increasing PatchTST capacity worsened relative performance against a linear benchmark.

record.problems: The empirical evaluation is on one EUR/USD dataset and reports one main PatchTST configuration; preliminary capacity comparisons are qualitative and lack sizes and numerical results. The text gives inconsistent descriptions of the error ratio (≈ 1.71 versus 'nearly three times') and of the per-window fraction (≈ 0.92 versus approximately 94%). It does not report whether the PatchTST configuration interpolates its training data.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible claim-related results were omitted. Cited findings from other work were excluded.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep, threshold or peak.
No capacity sweep through or beyond interpolation, in any model class.
No variation of label noise or regularization, and no multiple peaks. Noise reuse is argued only theoretically for 1-NN.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' with a V4 'challenges' label is rejected. The paper says double-descent results hold when sufficient structure is present and positions its regime as different, not as refuting them. Its internal inconsistencies (1.71 described as 'nearly three times'; 0.92 versus 94%) are correctly flagged in the record.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or fall-rise-fall curve; the qualitative capacity statement does not locate an interpolation threshold or peak.
No comparison across training-set sizes near an interpolation threshold.
The paper compares a linear class with a class containing interpolating predictors, but does not sweep capacity or demonstrate the full curve, its interpolation point, or a classical U-shaped curve.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across model size, epochs, and sample size.
The paper proposes a noise-reuse/variance explanation, but does not test peak dependence on label noise or regularization, multiple peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
No alternative effective-parameter count is measured against the shape of a descent curve.

n large enough for the stated comparison
Nearest-neighbor-type predictor reproducing a training output

rows.value: E∥Yt(H) − f̂n(Xt(L))∥₂² ≥ 2Hσ²; the paper states this is strictly larger than the linear predictor's error for n large enough.
rows.note: The comparison is a theoretical result under the paper's stated regularity assumptions, not a measured model-size sweep.
rows.check: This is a single interpolating predictor, the classical 1-NN noise-doubling bound, with no capacity axis. V4 concerns risk falling again as capacity grows past interpolation, which this result cannot show. The state 'reversed' is unjustified.

rows.value: E∥Yt(H) − f̂nℓ(Xt(L))∥₂² = Hσ² + O(Hσ²/n); the paper states it is strictly smaller than the interpolator's error for n large enough.
rows.note: This comparator is part of the theoretical result that the richer interpolating predictor can have strictly worse expected error.
rows.check: A comparator in a two-point theoretical comparison. There is no capacity sweep, so it does not bear on any version.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Theoretical comparison in Proposition 2 under its stated martingale-type and regularity assumptions
reader_labels.reason: The rich class contains an interpolating predictor whose expected error is bounded below by 2Hσ², while the linear predictor has error Hσ² + O(Hσ²/n), and the paper states the former is strictly worse for n large enough (r1–r2).
